items.text: What Michigan law and MCL sections govern adjuster licensing?
Chapter 12 of the Insurance Code of 1956, Act 218, MCL 500.1200 through 500.1247.
Is 'adjuster' or 'adjuster for the insured' defined in MCL 500.1201-1206?

No. MCL 500.1201 defines agent, agent of the insured, agent of the insurer, insurance producer, negotiate, sell, solicit, and other producer terms, but none of the three terms adjuster, adjuster for the insured, or independent adjuster appears as a defined term anywhere in 1201 through 1206.
Quote MCL 500.1222(1), the core adjuster prohibition.

'A person shall not adjust loss or damage under a policy of insurance or advertise, solicit business, or hold himself or herself out to the public as an adjuster unless he or she is licensed as an adjuster.'
How many exemptions does MCL 500.1222(2) list, and how are they lettered?
Exactly five, lettered (a) through (e). There is no sixth exemption for contractors, family members, or volunteers.
Which profession is exempt from adjuster licensure under MCL 500.1222(2)(a)?
A person admitted to the practice of law in this state, meaning a Michigan-licensed attorney.
Why is a company claims adjuster exempt from licensure under MCL 500.1222(2)(c)?
Because they are 'an employee or manager of an authorized insurer adjusting loss or damage under a policy issued by the insurer,' exempt due to their employment relationship, not a separate license.
What does MCL 500.1222(2)(d) exempt?
A licensed insurance producer to whom claim authority has been granted by an insurer.
Under MCL 500.1224(2), how long does the commissioner have to decide a completed adjuster license application?
60 days after receipt of a properly completed application, and the exam requirement may be waived for someone licensed as an adjuster within the preceding 12 months.
Quote MCL 500.1224(4) verbatim.

'The commissioner shall not issue a license to act as an adjuster to a person who is employed by, owns stock in, is an officer or director of, or in any other manner is connected with, a fire repair contractor.'
TRAP: Is 'fire repair contractor' defined anywhere in Chapter 12?

No. Chapter 12 uses the phrase in MCL 500.1224(4) without defining it. DIFS's Guldshtadt Final Decision cross-references MCL 500.1200 and MCL 338.41(1), but those sections define 'good moral character,' not 'fire repair contractor.'
Quote the fee cap in MCL 500.1226(3).
'An adjuster for the insured shall not charge a rate for his or her services which exceeds 10% of the amount paid by the insurer in settlement of the loss.'
What three requirements does MCL 500.1226(4) impose before an adjuster for the insured may serve a client?

A written contract, on a form approved by the commissioner, must exist before any services are provided; a contract signed within 48 hours of the loss is voidable at the insured's option for 10 days after signing; and a copy must be given to the insured when the contract is executed.
Under MCL 500.1227(1), when may an adjuster for an insured NOT solicit a loss?
During the progress of the loss-producing occurrence, or while the fire department or its representatives are engaged at the damaged premises.
What conduct does MCL 500.1232 (insurance counselor) require a license for?

Auditing or abstracting insurance policies, or providing advice, counsel, or opinion about the benefits, coverage, terms, value, effect, advantages, or disadvantages of a policy, or advertising or holding out as an insurance counselor.
TRAP: Does MCL 500.1232 flatly ban a non-licensee from ever using the word 'consultant' in an insurance context?

No. The ban is conditional: a non-licensee 'shall not use terms such as consultant, consulting services, or any other language in a way which implies that he or she is a licensed insurance counselor.' The bigger exposure is the section's separate ban on unlicensed advice about a policy's coverage or value.
Who is exempt from MCL 500.1232's insurance counselor license requirement?
A person admitted to the practice of law in this state, and the customary advice offered by a licensed insurance agent.
What does MCL 500.1236 require before an insurance counselor renders services?
A written agreement, signed by both counselor and client, outlining the work and stating the fee; the counselor must retain a copy for at least 2 years and make it available to DIFS on request.
Under MCL 500.1242(1), what must the commissioner do when refusing to grant an adjuster license?
Give written notice setting forth the basis for refusal; if the applicant requests a hearing within 30 days, the commissioner must promptly conduct one.
Under MCL 500.1242(2), on what grounds may the commissioner suspend or revoke an adjuster's license?
Failing to maintain the standards required for initial licensing, or violating any provision of the Insurance Code, after notice and opportunity for a hearing.
What authority does MCL 500.1242(4) give the commissioner, and what is the required timeline?

Authority to summarily suspend a license without a prior hearing if emergency action is needed to protect the public; if a hearing is requested, it must be held within 20 days of the suspension's effective date, with a decision announced within 30 days after the hearing concludes.
Under MCL 500.1244(1)(a), what are the two civil fine tiers per violation, and the total cap per order?
Up to $1,000 per violation normally, rising to up to $5,000 per violation if the person knew or should have known of the violation, with a hard cap of $50,000 per order.
Under MCL 500.1244(3), what is the fine and cap for knowingly violating a cease-and-desist order?
Up to $20,000 per violation, with a cap of $100,000 per order, plus suspension or revocation of the license.
Which vendor does DIFS contract to administer Michigan's adjuster licensing exams?
PSI Services LLC, through test-takers.psiexams.com/midifs, per the DIFS Examination Information page and the PSI Candidate Information Bulletin.
What is Michigan's resident adjuster application/license fee, per DIFS?

$15.00 plus a $5.00 transaction fee, filed as an Electronic Resident Licensing application through NIPR; the application stays valid 6 months, and the exam must be passed within that window or the applicant must reapply and pay again.
What is the flat examination fee PSI charges for any Michigan insurance licensing exam, including adjuster exams?
$41, non-refundable and non-transferable, valid one year from the date of payment.
What are the time limit, item count, and passing cut score for Michigan's Public Adjuster exam?
2 hours, 100 items, 71% passing cut score.
TRAP: Does Chapter 12 or the DIFS adjuster licensing page impose a continuing-education requirement on adjusters?

No CE requirement for adjusters was found in Chapter 12 or on the DIFS licensing page opened this run. Producers, a different license category, do have a CE requirement under MCL 500.1204c; do not import that rule onto adjusters.
TRAP: Is a surety bond required to hold a Michigan adjuster license?
No bond requirement for adjusters was found in MCL 500.1222-1247 or on the DIFS licensing page opened this run. Do not assert a bond requirement without a source.
Who is Aleksandr Guldshtadt and what license did he hold?
A licensed non-resident adjuster for the insured, qualified in Fire and Other Hazards, affiliated with an adjusting firm called Nationwide Insurance Claims Advocates (NICA).
When was Guldshtadt's license summarily suspended, and under what statutory authority?
November 3, 2025, under MCL 500.1242(4), the summary-suspension-for-emergency-action authority.
When was the Guldshtadt Final Decision issued, and what were the two sanctions?
April 1, 2026; a $50,000 civil fine and revocation of his adjuster license (System ID No. 1232766).
How was Guldshtadt found 'connected with' a fire repair contractor, and which subsections did DIFS actually cite?

He was listed as CEO of Evolve Construction & Restoration on its California corporate filings and as its registered agent on its Michigan filings, even though he told a DIFS investigator he did not partner with contractors. Note the citation precision: the categorical licensing bar is MCL 500.1224(4), but the Final Decision's conclusion cited MCL 500.1224(3) and MCL 500.1242(2), failure to maintain the standards required for initial licensing.
What fee percentage did many of Guldshtadt's unapproved contracts charge, against the MCL 500.1226(3) cap?
35%, more than triple the 10% cap in MCL 500.1226(3).
Was the Guldshtadt Final Decision based on a contested hearing or a default record?

A default record. Guldshtadt never requested a hearing on the summary suspension or on the Administrative Complaint by the stated deadline of March 2, 2026, so DIFS accepted the unchallenged allegations in the Complaint as true.
What is the citation and publication status of Tredenick v Nationwide Agribusiness (Prime Adjusting Service)?
Michigan Court of Appeals No. 349887, decided April 8, 2021, per curiam, UNPUBLISHED. Under MCR 7.215(C)(1), unpublished opinions are persuasive only, not binding precedent.
Quote the Tredenick court's holding on quantum meruit.

'Given that Prime failed to meet the statutory condition precedent to perform public adjuster services, there is no inherit [sic] inequity in denying it payment for those services.' The opinion prints 'inherit'; do not quote it as 'inherent.'
Quote Florida's anti-relabeling clause in Fla. Stat. 626.854(1).

A public adjuster is anyone who prepares, completes, or files an insurance claim for an insured, or negotiates a settlement, for compensation, 'regardless of how that person describes or presents his or her services.'
What contractor safe harbor does Fla. Stat. 626.854(16) provide that Michigan's statute does not?

A licensed contractor may discuss or explain a bid for construction or repair with the property owner or insurer, for the usual and customary fees stated in the contractor's own contract, without becoming an unlicensed public adjuster.
TRAP: Does Michigan's MCL 500.1222 contain a 'regardless of how described' anti-relabeling clause like Florida's?
No. Michigan has no such sentence in 1222. The relabeling problem in Michigan runs through MCL 500.1232's conditional word-ban on 'consultant,' not through the adjuster-prohibition statute itself.

A restoration contractor writes a full repair estimate for a homeowner's fire claim, submits it directly to the carrier, and negotiates the settlement amount for a percentage fee. Is a contractor exemption available under MCL 500.1222?

No. MCL 500.1222(2) lists exactly five exemptions (attorney, marine average adjuster, insurer employee, producer with claim authority, supervised data-entry clerk); there is no contractor exemption. This conduct sits inside the prohibited 'adjust loss or damage' and 'hold himself or herself out as an adjuster' language of 1222(1).
Jacob is an officer of a Michigan restoration contracting company. Can he obtain a Michigan adjuster license while holding that role?

No. MCL 500.1224(4) categorically bars the commissioner from issuing an adjuster license to anyone employed by, owning stock in, an officer or director of, or otherwise connected with a fire repair contractor. This is a licensing bar that applies before any conduct is examined.
A public adjuster's contract, signed 24 hours after a house fire, omits the required 48-hour/10-day voidability sentence. Under Tredenick, what happens to the adjuster's fee claim?

The adjuster loses the fee entirely, and quantum meruit (reasonable-value payment) is also unavailable, even for a licensed adjuster whose contract was defective in one clause. Tredenick holds there is 'no inherit [sic] inequity' in denying payment when the statutory condition precedent, a DIFS-approved contract, was never met.
An adjuster for the insured charges a client 15% of the insurer's settlement payment. Which statute is violated, and by how much does the fee exceed the cap?
MCL 500.1226(3), which caps the fee at 10% of the amount paid by the insurer. The 15% fee exceeds the cap by 5 percentage points, or 50% over the legal maximum.
A contractor labels a fee tied to a percentage of the insurance recovery a 'consulting fee for our experience as contractors' in the contract. Does the word 'consulting' alone violate MCL 500.1232?

Not automatically. The 1232 word-ban only applies where the term implies the person is a licensed insurance counselor. But pairing the label with a percentage-of-recovery fee and claim submission still risks the section's separate ban on unlicensed advice about a policy's value, and risks MCL 500.1222 for the underlying adjusting conduct.
An adjuster for the insured wants to pay an unlicensed telemarketer a commission for every referral that becomes a signed claim contract. Does MCL 500.1226(1) allow this?

No. The telemarketer would have to be a person the adjuster regularly employs AND who is separately licensed as an adjuster. An unlicensed commissioned referral source does not qualify under either prong.
DIFS believes an adjuster's ongoing conduct is actively harming consumers and needs to stop today, before a hearing can be scheduled. What authority applies, and what happens next procedurally?

MCL 500.1242(4), summary suspension without a prior hearing, effective on the date specified or on service, whichever is later. If the licensee requests a hearing, it must occur within 20 days of the suspension's effective date, and the commissioner must announce a decision within 30 days after the hearing concludes.
An insured signs a public adjuster contract at the loss address on the same day as the fire. What right does MCL 500.1226(4) give the insured, and for how long?
Because the contract was executed within 48 hours of the loss-producing occurrence, the insured may void it at their own option for 10 days after execution, for any reason.
A public adjuster's contract only marks the building and contents coverages as its scope, but the carrier also pays a loss-of-use benefit. Can the adjuster charge 10% of the loss-of-use payment too?

No. DIFS's FAQ confirms the 10% cap applies only to payments made under the coverages actually marked on the contract; a PA hired only for building and contents cannot also charge on loss-of-use or other unmarked coverages.
A Michigan-licensed attorney negotiates a fire claim settlement for a client and charges a contingency fee. Does the attorney need an adjuster license or an insurance counselor license?

No. MCL 500.1222(2)(a) exempts attorneys admitted to practice law in Michigan from the adjuster license requirement, and MCL 500.1232 likewise does not apply to a person admitted to the practice of law. The State Bar's own licensing and ethics regime governs the attorney's conduct instead.

A Michigan contractor wants to discuss their own repair bid directly with the insurer, for their usual contract price. Does Michigan's statute give this an explicit safe harbor the way Florida's 626.854(16) does?

No explicit statutory safe harbor exists in Michigan the way Florida's 626.854(16) states it. The Michigan boundary is drawn case by case through MCL 500.1222 enforcement and cases like Guldshtadt and Tredenick, not through a dedicated statutory carve-out for contractors.
An adjuster's license application was submitted through NIPR six months ago and the applicant still has not scheduled the PSI exam. What happens to the application and fee?
The application expires; per DIFS's licensing page, if the exam is not passed within six months, the applicant must submit a new license application and fee and reschedule the examination.
A company adjuster who is a full-time W-2 employee of an authorized insurer handles a claim on a policy that insurer issued. Does this person need a separate adjuster license?
No. MCL 500.1222(2)(c) exempts an employee or manager of an authorized insurer adjusting loss or damage under a policy issued by that same insurer.
A public adjuster refers a homeowner to a specific repair contractor and receives a payment from that contractor for the referral. Which statute does this violate?
MCL 500.1227(2), which prohibits an adjuster for an insured from collecting or attempting to collect a fee or charge from a repair contractor for obtaining repair work for the contractor.
An adjuster for the insured shows up at a house fire while the fire department is still on scene and tries to sign the homeowner to a contract on the spot. Is this legal under MCL 500.1227(1)?
No. MCL 500.1227(1) prohibits an adjuster for an insured from soliciting a loss during the progress of the loss-producing occurrence or while fire department personnel are engaged at the premises.
A homeowner is worried an adjuster's advance of cash before the claim is settled will obligate them somehow. What does MCL 500.1227(3) say about this practice?
It is prohibited outright: an adjuster for an insured shall not advance money or any other valuable thing to an insured pending adjustment of a claim.

A licensed adjuster's contract with a client was never on a DIFS-approved form at all, not even a modified one. Under Tredenick's reasoning, is the outcome better or worse than the Tredenicks' case, where only one clause was missing?

Worse. Tredenick's own reasoning treats the DIFS-approved-form requirement as an 'absolute bar' on providing services; an adjuster using no approved form at all has an even weaker position than an adjuster whose form was approved but missing one clause.
DIFS finds an adjuster knowingly violated a cease-and-desist order issued under MCL 500.1244(1). What is the maximum fine per violation and per order under 1244(3)?
Up to $20,000 per violation, capped at $100,000 total per order, plus the license may be suspended or revoked.
Guldshtadt's $50,000 fine equals the aggregate cap in which subsection, and under which statutes did DIFS order it?

The $50,000 figure equals the aggregate order cap in MCL 500.1244(1)(a). DIFS ordered it under MCL 500.2038, 500.1244, and 500.150, for violations of MCL 500.1222, 500.1226, 500.1244, 500.2026, 500.2003, and 500.4503.
A public adjuster hires unlicensed door-knockers affiliated with a contractor to present its DIFS-approved contract to homeowners. Guldshtadt's order cited this as a violation of which section?
MCL 500.1226(1), because unlicensed affiliates were used to aid in soliciting or adjusting a loss, not the adjuster's own regularly-employed and separately-licensed staff.

A homeowner refuses to sign a contract with a public adjuster and instead pays a licensed contractor to just write an estimate for the homeowner's own use, with no submission to the carrier or negotiation by the contractor. Under the statutory text reviewed this run, does this alone trigger MCL 500.1222?

The estimate-only, no-submission, no-negotiation scenario is not squarely addressed by 1222's text, which prohibits adjusting, advertising as an adjuster, or holding out as one; writing an estimate for the owner's own use, without submitting or negotiating it, falls outside those three triggers on the facts as stated. Any broader claim about what is or is not adjusting beyond this is analysis, not verified statutory text.
